name: Anxiety or constant worry
summary: Everyone feels anxious sometimes, but anxiety that is strong, hard to control or lasts a long time can affect daily life. It is common and there are effective ways to manage and treat it.
redFlags: Thoughts of ending your life or harming yourself, or feeling you might act on them
Chest pain, shortness of breath or feeling faint that you are not sure is anxiety
You feel you are in immediate danger or cannot keep yourself safe
urgentFlags: Anxiety so severe you cannot carry out daily tasks or leave the house
Thoughts of self-harm or suicide without a plan to act on them
Using alcohol or drugs to cope and feeling out of control

commonCauses.title: Stressful life events
commonCauses.detail: Work, money, relationships, health worries or big changes can trigger anxiety.

commonCauses.title: Generalised anxiety disorder (GAD)
commonCauses.detail: Ongoing, excessive worry about many things that is hard to control.

commonCauses.title: Past experiences
commonCauses.detail: Difficult or traumatic experiences can make anxiety more likely.

commonCauses.title: Caffeine, alcohol and drugs
commonCauses.detail: Stimulants and withdrawal can cause or worsen anxiety.

commonCauses.title: Physical health conditions
commonCauses.detail: An overactive thyroid and some medicines can cause anxiety-like symptoms.

selfCare: Try slow breathing: breathe in gently through your nose and out slowly through your mouth
Be physically active most days
Talk to someone you trust about how you feel
Try evidence-based self-help such as online cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) resources
Keep regular sleep, cut down on caffeine and alcohol
avoid: Using alcohol, drugs or smoking to cope
Avoiding situations that make you anxious, which can make anxiety worse over time
Unregulated supplements marketed as anxiety cures
seeDoctorIf: Anxiety is affecting your daily life or causing you distress
Self-help has not helped after a few weeks
You have physical symptoms such as palpitations that worry you
You think you may have an anxiety disorder or panic attacks

name: Low mood or feeling depressed
summary: Low mood often lifts after a few days or weeks, especially with support. If you have felt low or lost interest in things for 2 weeks or more, it could be depression, which is common and treatable.
redFlags: Thoughts of ending your life, or making plans to
You have harmed yourself or feel you cannot keep yourself safe
You feel you are in immediate danger
urgentFlags: Thoughts of suicide or self-harm, even without a plan
Not eating or drinking, or unable to look after yourself
Seeing or hearing things others do not, or very unusual beliefs

commonCauses.title: Life events
commonCauses.detail: Loss, relationship problems, money worries, illness or loneliness.

commonCauses.title: Depression
commonCauses.detail: Persistent low mood or loss of interest for at least 2 weeks, often with poor sleep, appetite changes and tiredness.

commonCauses.title: After having a baby
commonCauses.detail: Postnatal depression can affect parents in the year after birth.

commonCauses.title: Seasonal changes
commonCauses.detail: Some people feel lower in the darker winter months.

commonCauses.title: Alcohol, drugs and health conditions
commonCauses.detail: These can cause or worsen low mood.

selfCare: Talk to someone you trust about how you are feeling
Try to stay active, even with a short daily walk
Keep a routine with regular meals and sleep
Set small, achievable goals each day
Try evidence-based self-help such as CBT-based books or online programmes
avoid: Using alcohol or drugs to cope
Withdrawing from friends and family completely
Stopping prescribed antidepressants suddenly without advice
seeDoctorIf: You have felt low or lost interest in things for more than 2 weeks
Low mood is affecting work, relationships or daily life
Self-help is not working
You feel low after having a baby

sources.label: NHS – Low mood, sadness and depression

name: Panic attacks
summary: A panic attack is a sudden rush of intense fear with physical symptoms such as a racing heart, sweating, shaking and breathlessness. Panic attacks are frightening but not dangerous, and usually peak within 10 minutes.
redFlags: Chest pain or pressure, especially spreading to the arm, neck or jaw, that you are not sure is panic
Severe breathlessness, blue lips or fainting
Thoughts of suicide or harming yourself
urgentFlags: Your first ever attack with chest pain or palpitations, even if it has passed
Panic attacks happening very often and stopping you from going out

commonCauses.title: Stress and anxiety
commonCauses.detail: Panic attacks often happen during stressful periods.

commonCauses.title: Panic disorder
commonCauses.detail: Repeated, unexpected attacks with fear of having another.

commonCauses.title: Triggers
commonCauses.detail: Caffeine, alcohol withdrawal, drugs and lack of sleep can trigger attacks.

commonCauses.title: Phobias and past trauma
commonCauses.detail: Particular situations or memories can set off panic.

selfCare: Remind yourself that the attack will pass and cannot harm you
Breathe slowly and deeply: in through your nose for a count of 4, out through your mouth for 4
Focus on something around you, such as things you can see and hear
Exercise regularly and cut down on caffeine and alcohol
Learn about panic using reputable self-help resources
avoid: Fighting the attack or trying to escape it
Avoiding places where attacks have happened
Breathing into a paper bag, which is no longer recommended
seeDoctorIf: You keep having panic attacks
You are avoiding places or situations in case you have an attack
Panic attacks are affecting work or relationships

name: Can't sleep (insomnia)
summary: Insomnia means regularly having trouble falling asleep, staying asleep or waking too early. It is common, often linked to stress, and usually improves by changing sleep habits.
redFlags: Not sleeping with thoughts of suicide or self-harm
Going days without sleep with racing thoughts, very high energy, or seeing or hearing things others do not
urgentFlags: Severe distress or inability to function because of lack of sleep
Sleep problems after starting or stopping a medicine, with feeling very unwell

commonCauses.title: Stress, anxiety and depression
commonCauses.detail: Worry and low mood are among the most common causes.

commonCauses.title: Sleep habits and environment
commonCauses.detail: Irregular hours, screens, a noisy or bright bedroom and naps.

commonCauses.title: Caffeine, alcohol and nicotine
commonCauses.detail: These disrupt sleep, especially later in the day.

commonCauses.title: Shift work and jet lag
commonCauses.detail: Disrupt the body clock.

commonCauses.title: Health problems
commonCauses.detail: Pain, needing to pee at night, menopause, sleep apnoea, restless legs and some medicines.

selfCare: Go to bed and get up at the same times every day
Keep your bedroom dark, quiet and cool
Avoid caffeine in the afternoon and evening, and limit alcohol
Wind down before bed and keep screens out of bed
If you cannot sleep, get up and do something calm, then return to bed when sleepy
Be physically active during the day, but not just before bed
avoid: Long daytime naps
Using alcohol to help you sleep
Relying on over-the-counter sleeping pills for more than a few nights
seeDoctorIf: Changing your sleep habits has not helped
You have had trouble sleeping for months
Insomnia is affecting your daily life
You snore loudly, stop breathing in your sleep or have restless legs

name: Snoring
summary: Snoring is very common and often harmless, but loud snoring with pauses in breathing or gasping can be a sign of sleep apnoea. Lifestyle changes often help.
redFlags: Someone cannot be woken, or is struggling to breathe while asleep
Snoring with choking that does not settle when the person wakes
urgentFlags: Being so sleepy during the day that you have nearly fallen asleep while driving

commonCauses.title: Being overweight
commonCauses.detail: Extra weight around the neck narrows the airway.

commonCauses.title: Alcohol and sleeping tablets
commonCauses.detail: Relax the throat muscles.

commonCauses.title: Sleeping on your back
commonCauses.detail: The tongue and soft tissues fall back.

commonCauses.title: Blocked nose
commonCauses.detail: Colds, allergies or nasal problems.

commonCauses.title: Obstructive sleep apnoea
commonCauses.detail: The airway repeatedly closes during sleep, causing pauses in breathing and gasping.

selfCare: Lose weight if you are overweight
Sleep on your side
Avoid alcohol for a few hours before bed
Stop smoking
Treat a blocked nose, for example with saline sprays
avoid: Sleeping tablets
Expensive anti-snoring devices before getting checked for sleep apnoea if you are very sleepy
seeDoctorIf: Someone has noticed you stop breathing, gasp or choke in your sleep
You feel very tired during the day
Snoring is affecting your life or your partner's sleep
Lifestyle changes have not helped

name: Pauses in breathing or gasping during sleep
summary: Stopping breathing, gasping or choking during sleep, often with loud snoring, can be a sign of obstructive sleep apnoea. It is common, treatable, and worth getting checked because it can affect your health and safety.
redFlags: Someone cannot be woken, or has blue or grey lips while asleep
Waking gasping with chest pain or severe breathlessness that does not settle
urgentFlags: Falling asleep or nearly falling asleep while driving
Sleepiness so severe you cannot stay awake during daily activities

commonCauses.title: Obstructive sleep apnoea
commonCauses.detail: The throat repeatedly narrows or closes during sleep.

commonCauses.title: Being overweight
commonCauses.detail: The biggest risk factor for sleep apnoea.

commonCauses.title: Alcohol, sedatives and smoking
commonCauses.detail: Make the airway more likely to collapse.

commonCauses.title: Large tonsils or nasal blockage
commonCauses.detail: A common cause in children.

selfCare: Lose weight if you are overweight
Sleep on your side
Avoid alcohol in the evening and stop smoking
Ask your partner to note how often pauses happen
avoid: Driving when you feel sleepy
Sleeping tablets or sedatives
Ignoring daytime sleepiness
seeDoctorIf: Someone has seen you stop breathing or gasp in your sleep
You wake up tired or with headaches
You feel very sleepy during the day
A child snores loudly with pauses in breathing

name: Nightmares or night terrors
summary: Nightmares are frightening dreams that wake you up; night terrors are episodes of screaming or thrashing while still asleep, mostly in children. Both are usually harmless, but frequent nightmares can be linked to stress or trauma.
redFlags: Thoughts of suicide or self-harm
Someone hurting themselves or others during a sleep episode
Jerking or stiffening during sleep that may be a seizure
urgentFlags: Nightmares after a traumatic event with severe distress during the day
Nightmares that started after a new medicine and are very distressing

commonCauses.title: Stress and anxiety
commonCauses.detail: Worries often show up in dreams.

commonCauses.title: Trauma and PTSD
commonCauses.detail: Repeated nightmares about a frightening event.

commonCauses.title: Medicines, alcohol and withdrawal
commonCauses.detail: Some medicines and stopping alcohol or drugs can cause vivid dreams.

commonCauses.title: Night terrors in children
commonCauses.detail: Common, usually harmless, and most children grow out of them.

commonCauses.title: Poor sleep
commonCauses.detail: Overtiredness and irregular sleep make both more likely.

selfCare: Keep regular sleep times and a calming bedtime routine
Cut down on alcohol and caffeine
Write down a recurring nightmare and imagine a different, calmer ending in the daytime
For a child's night terrors, stay calm and keep them safe without trying to wake them
avoid: Watching frightening content before bed
Waking a child during a night terror
seeDoctorIf: Nightmares happen often and affect your daytime life
Nightmares are linked to a traumatic experience
A child's night terrors happen several times a night or most nights

name: Stress or feeling overwhelmed
summary: Stress is the body's reaction to feeling under pressure. Short-term stress is normal, but long-lasting stress can affect sleep, mood and physical health.
redFlags: Thoughts of ending your life or harming yourself
Chest pain or pressure that you are not sure is stress
urgentFlags: Feeling unable to cope at all or to look after yourself
Drinking or using drugs heavily to cope

commonCauses.title: Work or study pressure
commonCauses.detail: Heavy workloads, deadlines and job insecurity.

commonCauses.title: Money and housing worries
commonCauses.detail: Common long-term sources of stress.

commonCauses.title: Relationships and caring
commonCauses.detail: Family conflict or caring for someone.

commonCauses.title: Big life changes
commonCauses.detail: Moving, bereavement, illness or a new baby.

selfCare: Break problems into smaller steps and focus on what you can change
Be physically active and spend time outdoors
Talk to friends, family or a support line
Try breathing exercises, mindfulness or relaxation
Protect time for sleep and things you enjoy
avoid: Using alcohol, smoking or drugs to cope
Taking on more than you can manage
Cutting yourself off from others
seeDoctorIf: Stress is affecting your sleep, mood or health for more than a few weeks
Self-help is not helping
You have physical symptoms such as headaches or palpitations that worry you

name: Anger or irritability
summary: Anger is a normal emotion, but frequent irritability or outbursts that are hard to control can affect relationships and wellbeing. It is often linked to stress, tiredness, low mood or anxiety.
redFlags: You feel you might seriously hurt yourself or someone else
Someone is in immediate danger from violence
Sudden personality change or aggression with confusion, headache or weakness
urgentFlags: Anger leading to hurting people or damaging things
Irritability with very little sleep, racing thoughts and unusually high energy
Thoughts of suicide or self-harm

commonCauses.title: Stress and tiredness
commonCauses.detail: Pressure and poor sleep make it harder to manage emotions.

commonCauses.title: Depression or anxiety
commonCauses.detail: Both can show up as irritability.

commonCauses.title: Alcohol and drugs
commonCauses.detail: Can lower self-control and worsen anger.

commonCauses.title: Hormonal changes
commonCauses.detail: Premenstrual changes and menopause can affect mood.

commonCauses.title: Past experiences
commonCauses.detail: Trauma can make anger more likely.

selfCare: Notice early signs such as a racing heart or clenched fists, and step away
Take slow breaths and count to 10 before responding
Exercise to release tension
Talk it through later when calm
Look into anger management courses or self-help programmes
avoid: Drinking alcohol or using drugs when angry
Driving when very angry
Bottling anger up until it explodes
seeDoctorIf: Anger is affecting your relationships, work or daily life
You feel irritable most of the time
You are worried about how you behave when angry

name: Thoughts of suicide
summary: If you are having thoughts of ending your life, you are not alone and help is available right now. Talking to someone can help you get through this moment.
redFlags: You have made plans or have the means to end your life
You feel you cannot keep yourself safe right now
You have taken an overdose or seriously harmed yourself
You are worried someone else is about to act on suicidal thoughts
urgentFlags: You are having thoughts of suicide, even without a plan
Suicidal thoughts are becoming more frequent or stronger
You have recently stopped or changed mental health medicine and feel worse

commonCauses.title: Depression and other mental health conditions
commonCauses.detail: Feeling hopeless or trapped is a symptom that treatment can help.

commonCauses.title: Overwhelming life events
commonCauses.detail: Loss, relationship breakdown, debt, abuse or isolation.

commonCauses.title: Alcohol and drugs
commonCauses.detail: Can make thoughts stronger and actions more impulsive.

commonCauses.title: Long-term pain or illness
commonCauses.detail: Living with ongoing illness can feel overwhelming.

selfCare: Call your local emergency number (such as 911, 999 or 112) if you are in immediate danger
Contact a crisis line now, for example 988 in the US and Canada or Samaritans on 116 123 in the UK and Ireland
Tell someone you trust how you are feeling and ask them to stay with you
Remove or move away from anything you could use to harm yourself
Make a safety plan listing people to call, reasons for living and safe places to go
avoid: Being alone if you feel unsafe
Drinking alcohol or using drugs
Making big decisions while you feel like this
seeDoctorIf: You have had suicidal thoughts recently, even if they have passed
You often feel hopeless or that others would be better off without you
You want help making a safety plan

name: Self-harm or urges to self-harm
summary: Self-harm is when someone hurts themselves on purpose, often as a way of coping with overwhelming feelings. Support is available, and you do not have to cope alone.
redFlags: A wound that is deep, bleeding heavily or will not stop bleeding
You have taken an overdose of tablets or swallowed something harmful, even if you feel fine
You have thoughts of ending your life or feel you cannot keep yourself safe
Feeling faint, drowsy or confused after self-harm
urgentFlags: A wound that may need stitches or is showing signs of infection
Urges to self-harm that are getting stronger or more frequent
Burns that are blistered or larger than a small area

commonCauses.title: Overwhelming emotions
commonCauses.detail: Anger, sadness, anxiety, numbness or self-hatred.

commonCauses.title: Difficult experiences
commonCauses.detail: Bullying, abuse, bereavement, relationship or school problems.

commonCauses.title: Mental health conditions
commonCauses.detail: Depression, anxiety, eating disorders and other conditions.

selfCare: Talk to someone you trust, or contact a crisis line, for example 988 in the US and Canada or Samaritans on 116 123 in the UK and Ireland
Clean minor wounds and keep them covered
Try to delay acting on the urge, and use distractions such as holding ice or going for a walk
Write down what triggers your urges to share with a professional
avoid: Being alone when urges are strong
Alcohol and drugs, which can make urges harder to resist
Keeping sharp objects or stockpiled medicines nearby
seeDoctorIf: You have self-harmed, even if the injury was minor
You want help finding other ways to cope
You are worried about someone else who is self-harming

name: Excessive daytime sleepiness
summary: Feeling very sleepy during the day is often caused by not getting enough good-quality sleep. When it happens despite enough sleep, it can be a sign of a sleep disorder or other health problem.
redFlags: Sudden drowsiness, confusion or difficulty waking someone
Drowsiness after a head injury
Drowsiness after taking too much medicine, alcohol or drugs
urgentFlags: Falling asleep or nearly falling asleep while driving
Sudden loss of muscle strength when laughing or with strong emotion
Sleepiness with breathlessness, morning headaches or swollen ankles

commonCauses.title: Not enough sleep
commonCauses.detail: Most adults need around 7 to 9 hours.

commonCauses.title: Sleep apnoea
commonCauses.detail: Interrupted breathing at night causes poor-quality sleep.

commonCauses.title: Medicines and alcohol
commonCauses.detail: Many medicines cause drowsiness.

commonCauses.title: Depression, anaemia or an underactive thyroid
commonCauses.detail: Can make you feel tired and sleepy.

commonCauses.title: Narcolepsy
commonCauses.detail: A rare condition causing sudden sleep attacks.

selfCare: Keep regular sleep times and aim for enough sleep
Get daylight and physical activity during the day
Limit alcohol and caffeine, especially in the evening
Take a short break and do not drive if you feel sleepy
avoid: Driving or using machinery when sleepy
Relying on caffeine or energy drinks to stay awake
seeDoctorIf: You feel very sleepy even after enough sleep
You snore loudly or someone has seen you stop breathing in your sleep
Sleepiness is affecting work, study or safety
You think a medicine is making you sleepy

name: Restless legs at night
aliases: urge to move legs at night
summary: Restless legs syndrome causes an overwhelming urge to move your legs, often with an uncomfortable crawling or tingling feeling, usually in the evening or at night. It can disrupt sleep but is not dangerous.
redFlags: Sudden weakness or numbness in a leg, or loss of bladder or bowel control
One leg suddenly painful, swollen, red or warm with breathlessness or chest pain
urgentFlags: One leg is painful, swollen, red or warm
Leg symptoms with a new rash, fever or feeling very unwell

commonCauses.title: Restless legs syndrome
commonCauses.detail: Often runs in families with no clear cause.

commonCauses.title: Low iron
commonCauses.detail: Iron deficiency is a common, treatable cause.

commonCauses.title: Pregnancy
commonCauses.detail: Often settles after the baby is born.

commonCauses.title: Medicines, caffeine and alcohol
commonCauses.detail: Some antidepressants, antihistamines and stimulants can make it worse.

commonCauses.title: Kidney disease or nerve damage
commonCauses.detail: Less common causes.

selfCare: Keep regular sleep habits
Cut down on caffeine, alcohol and smoking
Do gentle stretching or a warm bath before bed
Walk around or massage your legs when symptoms start
Do regular moderate exercise during the day
avoid: Caffeine and alcohol in the evening
Taking iron supplements without having your levels checked
seeDoctorIf: Symptoms are affecting your sleep
Symptoms are getting worse or happen most nights
You think a medicine might be causing it
You are pregnant and symptoms are troubling you

name: Sleepwalking or sleep talking
summary: Sleepwalking is when someone walks or does things while still asleep. It is common in children, usually harmless, and most grow out of it.
redFlags: Someone has been seriously injured while sleepwalking
Jerking, stiffening or tongue biting during sleep that may be a seizure
urgentFlags: Sleepwalking that puts the person or others at risk, such as leaving the house or using a car
Violent behaviour during sleep

commonCauses.title: Childhood development
commonCauses.detail: Common in children and often runs in families.

commonCauses.title: Lack of sleep and stress
commonCauses.detail: Overtiredness and anxiety make episodes more likely.

commonCauses.title: Alcohol and some medicines
commonCauses.detail: Including some sleeping tablets.

commonCauses.title: Other sleep problems
commonCauses.detail: Sleep apnoea or restless legs can trigger episodes.

selfCare: Keep regular sleep times and get enough sleep
Make the home safe: lock doors and windows and remove trip hazards
Gently guide a sleepwalker back to bed
Reduce stress and avoid alcohol before bed
avoid: Waking a sleepwalker suddenly
Sleeping on a top bunk or near stairs if you sleepwalk
seeDoctorIf: Sleepwalking happens often
It starts for the first time in adulthood
It causes injury or is disturbing others

name: Grief after a loss
summary: Grief is a natural response to losing someone or something important. It can bring sadness, anger, guilt, tiredness and poor sleep, and usually eases slowly over time.
redFlags: Thoughts of ending your life or wanting to join the person who died
You feel unable to keep yourself safe
urgentFlags: Unable to eat, drink or look after yourself
Using alcohol or drugs heavily to cope
Thoughts of self-harm

commonCauses.title: Bereavement
commonCauses.detail: The death of a family member, friend or pet.

commonCauses.title: Other losses
commonCauses.detail: Relationship breakdown, losing a job, a pregnancy loss or loss of health.

commonCauses.title: Complicated or prolonged grief
commonCauses.detail: Grief that stays very intense and stops you functioning for a long time.

selfCare: Talk about your feelings with people you trust
Allow yourself to feel the grief; there is no right way to grieve
Try to keep up regular meals, sleep and some activity
Contact a bereavement support service or group
Mark anniversaries and memories in a way that feels right
avoid: Using alcohol or drugs to block feelings
Making major decisions too soon
Isolating yourself completely
seeDoctorIf: Grief is not easing after several months or is getting worse
You cannot manage daily life
You have signs of depression such as hopelessness or loss of interest in everything

sources.label: NHS – Grief after bereavement or loss

name: Unwanted intrusive thoughts
summary: Most people have unwanted or upsetting thoughts sometimes. When they cause a lot of distress or lead to repeated checking, cleaning or other rituals, it may be obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD), which is treatable.
redFlags: Thoughts of suicide or harming yourself, with a wish or plan to act on them
You feel you cannot keep yourself or others safe
urgentFlags: Thoughts or rituals are stopping you eating, sleeping or leaving the house
Severe distress that you cannot manage

commonCauses.title: Normal intrusive thoughts
commonCauses.detail: Most people have them; they do not mean you want to act on them.

commonCauses.title: Obsessive compulsive disorder
commonCauses.detail: Obsessions cause anxiety, and compulsions are done to ease it.

commonCauses.title: Anxiety and stress
commonCauses.detail: Make unwanted thoughts more frequent and sticky.

commonCauses.title: After having a baby
commonCauses.detail: Upsetting thoughts about harm to the baby are common and treatable.

selfCare: Remind yourself that having a thought does not mean you want it or will act on it
Try not to push thoughts away or seek repeated reassurance, which can strengthen them
Use evidence-based self-help based on CBT
Be active and look after your sleep
avoid: Repeated checking, googling or seeking reassurance
Using alcohol or drugs to cope
seeDoctorIf: Thoughts or rituals take up more than an hour a day
They cause you a lot of distress
They are affecting work, relationships or daily life

name: Hearing voices or seeing things others cannot
summary: Hearing, seeing or believing things that others do not can be a sign of psychosis, but can also be caused by drugs, extreme lack of sleep, infection or other illness. It should be checked by a professional promptly.
redFlags: Voices telling you to harm yourself or others
Thoughts of suicide or feeling you cannot keep yourself safe
Sudden confusion, fever or drowsiness with hallucinations
Hallucinations after taking drugs or too much medicine, or during alcohol withdrawal
urgentFlags: New hallucinations or unusual beliefs
Being unable to look after yourself
Hallucinations in an older person, especially with new confusion

commonCauses.title: Psychosis
commonCauses.detail: Can happen with schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, severe depression or after a stressful event.

commonCauses.title: Drugs and alcohol
commonCauses.detail: Cannabis, stimulants and alcohol withdrawal can cause hallucinations.

commonCauses.title: Severe lack of sleep
commonCauses.detail: Can cause brief hallucinations.

commonCauses.title: Physical illness
commonCauses.detail: Infections, delirium, dementia and some medicines.

commonCauses.title: Falling asleep or waking up
commonCauses.detail: Brief hallucinations at these times are common and usually harmless.

selfCare: Tell someone you trust and ask them to help you get support
Avoid alcohol and recreational drugs
Try to keep regular sleep
If you have a care plan, follow it and contact your care team
avoid: Cannabis and other recreational drugs
Stopping prescribed medicines without advice
seeDoctorIf: You have heard or seen things others cannot, even if it has stopped
Friends or family are worried about changes in your thinking or behaviour
Brief hallucinations when falling asleep are frequent or distressing

name: Mood swings or extreme highs and lows
summary: Everyone's mood changes, but extreme highs (feeling very energetic, needing little sleep, racing thoughts) and lows that last days or weeks may be a sign of bipolar disorder or another condition that can be treated.
redFlags: Thoughts of suicide or harming yourself
Behaviour that puts you or others in immediate danger
Hearing voices or believing things that are clearly not true, with distress or risk
urgentFlags: Several days of very little sleep with racing thoughts and unusually high energy
Spending, driving or other behaviour that is out of character and risky
Very low mood after a period of feeling high

commonCauses.title: Stress, tiredness and life events
commonCauses.detail: Ordinary mood changes are often linked to these.

commonCauses.title: Hormonal changes
commonCauses.detail: Periods, pregnancy and the menopause can affect mood.

commonCauses.title: Bipolar disorder
commonCauses.detail: Episodes of depression and mania or hypomania lasting days to weeks.

commonCauses.title: Alcohol, drugs and medicines
commonCauses.detail: Can cause mood changes.

commonCauses.title: Personality disorders and ADHD
commonCauses.detail: Can involve rapid emotional changes.

selfCare: Keep a mood diary, including sleep, to spot patterns
Keep a regular routine for sleep, meals and activity
Avoid alcohol and recreational drugs
Ask someone close to tell you if they notice warning signs
avoid: Making big financial or life decisions when your mood is very high or low
Staying up all night
seeDoctorIf: Mood swings are affecting your life or relationships
You have periods of feeling unusually high or full of energy
You have had low mood for more than 2 weeks

name: Flashbacks or distress after a traumatic event
aliases: can't stop thinking about what happened
summary: After a frightening or traumatic event it is normal to feel shaken, have upsetting memories or struggle to sleep for a few weeks. If these continue for more than about a month, it may be post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), which is treatable.
redFlags: Thoughts of suicide or harming yourself
You are still in danger from the person or situation that hurt you
urgentFlags: Unable to cope with daily life or look after yourself
Using alcohol or drugs heavily to cope
A recent assault, including sexual assault, where you may need medical care or evidence collection

commonCauses.title: Normal reaction to trauma
commonCauses.detail: Many people have upsetting symptoms in the first few weeks that ease on their own.

commonCauses.title: Post-traumatic stress disorder
commonCauses.detail: Flashbacks, nightmares, avoidance and feeling on edge lasting more than a month.

commonCauses.title: Complex trauma
commonCauses.detail: Repeated trauma, such as abuse, can cause longer-lasting effects.

selfCare: Talk to people you trust about how you feel when you are ready
Keep a routine with regular meals, sleep and activity
Use grounding: notice what you can see, hear and touch during a flashback
Learn about common reactions to trauma from reputable sources
avoid: Using alcohol or drugs to cope
Being pushed to talk in detail about the event before you are ready
seeDoctorIf: Symptoms have lasted more than 4 weeks
Symptoms are severe or getting worse
You avoid people, places or things that remind you of the event

name: Worries about eating, weight or body shape
summary: Spending a lot of time worrying about weight, food or body shape, restricting food, bingeing or making yourself sick can be signs of an eating disorder. These are serious but treatable, and early help makes a difference.
redFlags: Fainting, chest pain, a very slow or irregular heartbeat, or confusion
Vomiting blood, or severe weakness after repeated vomiting
Thoughts of suicide or harming yourself
urgentFlags: Rapid weight loss or being unable to eat or drink
Feeling dizzy, very cold or very weak
Making yourself sick or using laxatives several times a day

commonCauses.title: Anorexia, bulimia and binge eating disorder
commonCauses.detail: The main types of eating disorder; they can affect anyone of any age, gender or size.

commonCauses.title: Stress and low self-esteem
commonCauses.detail: Controlling food can become a way to cope.

commonCauses.title: Social and family pressures
commonCauses.detail: Pressure about appearance, dieting culture or certain sports.

commonCauses.title: Other mental health conditions
commonCauses.detail: Anxiety, depression and OCD often occur alongside.

selfCare: Talk to someone you trust about your worries
Contact an eating disorder support line or service for advice
Try to eat regular meals rather than skipping meals or strict dieting
Unfollow social media accounts that make you feel worse about your body
avoid: Extreme diets, fasting or diet pills
Weighing yourself many times a day
Pro-eating disorder websites and communities
seeDoctorIf: Food, weight or body shape is taking over your thoughts
You are restricting, bingeing or purging
Someone close to you is worried about your eating
Your periods have stopped or you have lost a lot of weight

name: Loneliness
summary: Loneliness is a common feeling that can affect anyone at any age. Long-lasting loneliness can affect mood, sleep and health, but there are many ways to reconnect.
redFlags: Thoughts of ending your life or harming yourself
You feel unable to keep yourself safe
urgentFlags: Not eating, drinking or looking after yourself
An older or vulnerable person living alone who is not coping

commonCauses.title: Life changes
commonCauses.detail: Moving, retiring, bereavement, a break-up or becoming a parent or carer.

commonCauses.title: Health and mobility
commonCauses.detail: Illness, disability or hearing loss can make socialising harder.

commonCauses.title: Depression and social anxiety
commonCauses.detail: Can make it hard to reach out, and loneliness can worsen them.

commonCauses.title: Working from home or living alone
commonCauses.detail: Fewer day-to-day contacts.

selfCare: Reach out to one person: a call, message or short visit
Join a group, class, club or volunteering based on your interests
Spend time in shared spaces such as libraries, cafés or parks
Use befriending services or helplines
Look after sleep and stay active
avoid: Relying on alcohol to cope
Comparing yourself with others on social media
seeDoctorIf: Loneliness is affecting your mood, sleep or appetite
You think you may be depressed or anxious
Hearing loss or health problems are making it hard to socialise

sources.label: NHS – Low mood, sadness and depression

name: Health anxiety
summary: Health anxiety is spending so much time worrying about being ill that it affects your life. Constant checking, searching symptoms online and seeking reassurance can make the worry worse.
redFlags: Thoughts of suicide or harming yourself
Chest pain, difficulty breathing or other emergency symptoms, even if you think it may be anxiety
urgentFlags: Anxiety so severe you cannot carry out daily tasks

commonCauses.title: Anxiety
commonCauses.detail: People prone to worry are more likely to develop health anxiety.

commonCauses.title: Past illness
commonCauses.detail: Serious illness in yourself or someone close can trigger it.

commonCauses.title: Stress
commonCauses.detail: Health worries often increase during stressful times.

commonCauses.title: Online searching
commonCauses.detail: Searching symptoms can increase worry.

selfCare: Keep a diary of how often you check, search or seek reassurance, and gradually reduce it
Try to challenge your thoughts: what is the evidence for and against?
Stay busy and get regular exercise
Try CBT-based self-help resources
avoid: Repeatedly searching symptoms online
Checking your body over and over
Asking for the same reassurance many times
seeDoctorIf: Worry about your health is affecting your daily life
Self-help has not helped
You have a new symptom that has not been checked

name: Fear of social situations
summary: Social anxiety is an ongoing, overwhelming fear of social situations, such as meeting people or speaking in front of others. It is common, and talking therapies work well.
redFlags: Thoughts of suicide or harming yourself
urgentFlags: You are unable to leave the house or attend work or school
Using alcohol or drugs to cope with social situations and feeling out of control

commonCauses.title: Social anxiety disorder
commonCauses.detail: Intense fear of being judged or embarrassed that lasts a long time.

commonCauses.title: Past experiences
commonCauses.detail: Bullying, criticism or embarrassing events can contribute.

commonCauses.title: Shyness and temperament
commonCauses.detail: Some people are naturally more anxious in social situations.

commonCauses.title: Low mood or depression
commonCauses.detail: Can make social situations feel harder.

selfCare: Gradually face situations you fear in small steps
Prepare and practise for social situations
Focus on the conversation rather than on how you appear
Try CBT-based self-help resources
Use slow breathing to manage physical symptoms
avoid: Avoiding all social situations, which can make fear stronger
Using alcohol to cope
seeDoctorIf: Fear of social situations is affecting your life
You avoid work, study or seeing friends
Self-help has not helped
